doc.title: Butch Miles interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Life on the road with Basie: buses, day sheets, one-nighters
summary: He describes the band's travel schedule, paying for rooms, hit-and-run dates, and how the band always sounded good.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: You know that’s a very good question, because first of all I never heard a band other than Basie that could do that. And I’ve heard bands that tried, but they didn’t do it right. Maybe it was the combination of a specific Basie sound that had been borne over so many years and plus playing it so many times. I mean we must have played, in four and a half years “Jumpin’ at the Woodside” in four and a half years there were certain things you just could not get away from, you had to play. Of course “April in Paris” was a great deal, and always “One O’clock Jump.” It got to the point where you could play that totally sound asleep in a coma, you know, with a religious person standing over you saying this is it, you’re going to die, but first the outchorus to “One O’clock Jump.” Just go through the whole bit. It got to be like that, you sort of, we were on the road in such close proximity to each other all the time that so many of us began to think alike on the stage as far as the ensemble and the Basie arrangements went. There were, let me see there was 18 guys in the band, a vocalist, 19, and our band equipment manager. We used to call it the band boy but you don’t say that anymore. So that was like 20 people, then a bus driver, but we never knew who the bus driver was because we didn’t have a regular bus. Basie leased or chartered from Greyhound most the time. So we had different cats who were driving and whatnot going around. But you might start off the day by getting up at 6:00 in the morning to leave the hotel at 7:00 in the morning to make a 9:00 flight. So you’ve got to drive over to where the airport is, you know, everybody on the bus. Then you have everybody sitting around the airport. Then you get on the plane and you fly somewhere, everybody’s on the plane. Then you get off the plane and many times you’d have to get back on the bus and travel two or three hours to the destination. Then everybody goes in and gets something to eat. Then you show up, then you do the show, then more often than not you pack up and if you were lucky enough to have a hotel then you’d go back to the hotel and sometimes we’d get back on the bus and drive all night. You could make what we called the day sheet. If you drove all night, because we all paid our rooms and food, meals and all those expenses. Basie paid transportation. And if you could skip the hotel or the motel for that evening and driving all night until you get into the next town 6:30 or 7:00 in the morning, then the day sheet changes and they’ll charge you for that day. If you get in there at 1:30 in the morning, they’ll charge you for that day, and the next day. You know sort of like 1:30 in the morning is still the day before, even though it’s after midnight, so they change that day sheet at 6, 6:30. And many times we’d just try and save some money, the guys in the band trying to save a few extra
pennies and we’d do what’s called a hit and run. You’d hit the town that you were going in and then back on the bus and run to the next town. We had a lot of fun that way though. Yeah, we did.

Yeah. But you know I’ve said this all my life. Four and a half years — blizzards, rain storms, getting lost, yeah we got lost all the time, the bus drivers didn’t know where to go and we couldn’t tell them, that’s what we hired him, Basie hired him for, to get us there. And getting to places that we really didn’t want to be, sometimes no food, sometimes no overcoat, just a whole bunch of stuff I never ever, ever heard the band sound bad. Never. Four and a half years of one-nighters. They always sounded good. Many nights they were great, and some nights they were just unbelievable. And you never could figure that out. A lot of times you’d have four or five guys down with the flu. And everybody’s tired and they haven’t had a chance to shave and you’re all kind of crummy and stuff like that. The band would roar. Just incredible. Then there were some nights where everything was fine, the guys were rested, it was a beautiful job the whole bit, and the band was good, it wasn’t bad, but it wasn’t like that other night. You could always tell the difference. Maybe I’m not on, or somebody didn’t make the note or something doesn’t sound right or the rhythm section isn’t really locking in for some reason. You know, I’m not locking in with Freddie and John, whichever John it might be. And there were just some nights like that. But the band always sounded good. It was such a pleasure. You know I’m going to have to get out of here —
